extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply Robert E. Park's criteria for what counts as news — the features that make an event communicable, memorable, and likely to circulate in the public sphere. Useful for judging news selection, news framing, and news production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transience / ephemeral quality
rubrics_metrics.description: News also has a point characteristic of its transient and ephemeral quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News is a perishable commodity: it circulates only while it has 'news interest.' Once published and its significance recognized, what was news becomes history. Different types of news have different timespans (e.g., a 'flash' versus a continuing story). Editors must account for this perishability when selecting and sequencing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / present orientation (the 'specious present')
rubrics_metrics.description: News, as a form of knowledge, is not primarily concerned either with the past or with the future but rather with the present—what some psychologists call 'the specious present.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters focus on the actual, present condition of affairs; news's value derives from its immediacy. Material that illuminates current events or conditions has higher news value than retrospective analysis, unless the latter helps understand the present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-centeredness (focus on discrete events rather than causal sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter, as distinguished from a historian, seeks merely to record each single event as it occurs and is concerned with the past and future only insofar as these throw light on what is actual and present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News emphasizes isolated, time-and-space-located events rather than systematic causal or teleological explanation. Depth and historical linkage are the historian's task; the reporter's is to make the single event comprehensible and interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness / novelty (departure from routine)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the unexpected that happens. Since what happens makes news, it follows that news is always or mainly concerned with the unusual and the unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors favor departures from daily routine or customary ritual because such deviations attract attention. Even trivial happenings become news if they are appreciably novel for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest / ability to 'make people talk'
rubrics_metrics.description: News has been described ... as 'something that will make people talk.' The ordinary reader will read short, striking items that have human interest rather than long expositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that arouse emotion (pity, terror, amusement, astonishment) or that embody human drama are more likely to be read, repeated, and remembered. Examples: striking anecdotes, tragedies, or triumphs that assume ideal significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity, readability, and ease of comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: A newsitem, as every newspaperman knows, is read in inverse ratio to its length. News comes in the form of small, independent communications that can be easily and rapidly comprehended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep items concise and modular. Readers prefer short, compact communications that can be quickly understood and shared; long articles compete poorly unless they demonstrate exceptional interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public publication / authentication (distinguishes news from rumor)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that a report of current events may have the quality of news, it should not merely circulate ... but should be published, if need be, by the town crier or the public press. Such public publication tends to give news something of the character of a public document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named, dated, and place-stamped reports that allow verification are treated as authentic news; anonymous or undocumented reports tend to mutate into rumor or legend. Publication subjects a claim to public scrutiny and stamps it with communal acceptance (or rejection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Checkability / disclosure of source details
rubrics_metrics.description: When reports of current events are published with the names, dates, and places which make it possible for anyone concerned to check them, the atmosphere of legend is dispelled and what is fact is reduced to fact until corrected by later reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide verifiable facts (who, when, where) to strengthen credibility. Lack of such detail fosters circulation as rumor and undermines news authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative news value / competition among items
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason for this is that the news value is relative, and an event that comes later may, and often does, diminish the value of an event that turned up earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News selection is competitive and dynamic: editors must prioritize items because later events can eclipse earlier ones. Editors keep flexible formats (anecdotes, short items) that can be pushed aside for hotter stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to public attention and social tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Public attention ... is wavering, unsteady, and easily distracted. Exclusive attention to some things inhibits responses to others, resulting in a limitation of the range and character of the news to which a society will respond collectively or individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the current focus and tension of the public; in times of heightened social tension the range of items the public will attend to narrows, and the influence of dominant persons or issues rises. News selection should reflect and manage public focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secularity and pragmatic interest
rubrics_metrics.description: News is a purely secular phenomenon ... It is something that brings about sudden and decisive changes; news is pragmatic rather than appreciative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News tends to exclude the sacred/ritual domain and emphasize worldly events with practical consequences. Select items that have tangible or pragmatic relevance to readers' lives and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics the public is prepared for (expected categories but unpredictable specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The events that have made news in the past ... are actually the expected things: births and deaths, weddings and funerals, the conditions of the crops and of business, war, politics, and the weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even routine subject-areas can yield news when they produce unpredictable or consequential specifics. Coverage should pay attention to those domains the audience cares about because they are where unexpected incidents will matter most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function: circulation fosters public opinion and political action
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which news circulates determines the extent to which the members of a society participate in its political action. It is upon the interpretation of present events, i.e., news, that public opinion rests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news not only by its intrinsic features but also by its potential to circulate and shape collective judgments; high-circulation items have greater capacity to form public opinion and influence political behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability (ease of transmission and repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first typical reaction of an individual to the news is likely to be a desire to repeat it to someone. This makes conversation, arouses further and perhaps starts a discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer items that are easily retellable and memorizable. The more readily a piece of news can be shared in ordinary conversation, the more likely it is to spread and to function as public knowledge.
